question: Will our bodies rise?

answers.label: Yes: the same body will rise, transformed and glorified
A spiritual body will rise, not this flesh

overview.text: From the first letters after the New Testament, Christians taught that God will raise our bodies as he raised Christ's: Clement points to day and night and the seed; Polycarp to Christ as the pattern.
Against pagan scorn and Gnostic denial, Athenagoras and Tertullian defended the resurrection of this flesh, "all of it, the very same, entire".

Origen and Methodius then argued over what rises: Origen kept the body's form while its matter flows away, and Methodius answered that God melts his statue down only to cast the same work again. Augustine filled in the picture: every body restored whole, at the measure of its youth, with no deformity left.

quotes.author: Clement of Rome
quotes.english: Let us consider, beloved, how the Master continually shows us the resurrection to come, of which he made the Lord Jesus Christ the first fruits by raising him from the dead. Let us look, beloved, at the resurrection that happens at each season. Day and night show us resurrection: the night falls asleep, the day rises; the day departs, night comes on. Let us take the crops: how and in what way does the sowing happen?
quotes.original: Κατανοήσωμεν, ἀγαπητοί, πῶς ὁ δεσπότης ἐπιδείκνυται διηνεκῶς ἡμῖν τὴν μέλλουσαν ἀνάστασιν ἔσεσθαι, ἧς τὴν ἀπαρχὴν ἐποιήσατο τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστήσας. ἴδωμεν, ἀγαπητοί. τὴν κατὰ καιρὸν γινομένην ἀνάστασιν. ἡμέρα καὶ νὺξ ἀνάστασιν ἡμῖν δηλοῦσιν: κοιμᾶται ἡ νύξ, ἀνίσταται ἡ ἡμέρα: ἡ ἡμέρα ἄπεισιν, νὺξ ἐπέρχεται. λάβωμεν τοὺς καρπούς: ὁ σπόρος πῶς καὶ τίνα τρόπον γίνεται;
quotes.context: Clement goes on to the seed and to the phoenix (chapter 25) as signs of the resurrection.

quotes.author: Polycarp of Smyrna
quotes.english: ... believing in him who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead and gave him glory and a throne at his right hand ... who comes as judge of the living and the dead ... And he who raised him from the dead will raise us also, if we do his will and walk in his commandments.
quotes.original: πιστεύσαντες εἰς τὸν ἐγείραντα τὸν κύριον ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν καὶ δόντα αὐτῷ δόξαν καὶ θρόνον ἐκ δεξιῶν αὐτοῦ ... ὃς ἔρχεται κριτὴς ζώντων καὶ νεκρῶν ... ὁ δὲ ἐγείρας αὐτὸν ἐκ νεκρῶν καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐγερεῖ, ἐὰν ποιῶμεν αὐτοῦ τὸ θέλημα
quotes.context: Christ's resurrection as the pattern and promise of ours.

quotes.author: Athenagoras
quotes.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead
quotes.english: If at their first making he created human bodies and their elements when they did not exist, he will raise them just as easily when they have been dissolved, however that happens; for this too is equally possible for him.
quotes.original: Εἰ γὰρ μὴ ὄντα κατὰ τὴν πρώτην σύστασιν ἐποίησε τὰ τῶν ἀνθρώπων σώματα καὶ τὰς τούτων ἀρχάς, καὶ διαλυθέντα, καθ᾿ ὃν ἂν τύχῃ τρόπον, ἀναστήσει μετὰ τῆς ἴσης εὐμαρείας· ἐπ᾿ ἴσης γὰρ αὐτῷ καὶ τοῦτο δυνατόν.
quotes.context: Athenagoras answers the pagan objection about bodies eaten by animals or scattered.

quotes.author: Tertullian
quotes.work: On the Resurrection of the Flesh
quotes.english: So the flesh will rise: all of it, the very same, entire.
quotes.original: Resurget igitur caro, et quidem omnis, et quidem ipsa, et quidem integra.
quotes.context: The same flesh, not another body.

quotes.author: Origen of Alexandria
quotes.english: Our bodies are to be thought of as falling into the earth like a grain. There is a principle lodged in them that holds the bodily substance together. However dead the bodies may be, and corrupted and scattered, at God's word that same principle, which is always kept safe in the body's substance, will raise them from the earth and restore and repair them, just as the power in a grain of wheat, after its corruption and death, repairs and restores the grain into the body of the stalk and the ear.
quotes.original: Ita namque etiam nostra corpora velut granum cadere in terram putanda sunt: quibus insita ratio ea, quae substantiam continet corporalem, quamvis emortua fuerint corpora, et corrupta atque dispersa, verbo tamen Dei ratio illa ipsa, quae semper in substantia corporis salva est, erigat ea de terra, et restituat ac reparet, sicut ea virtus, quae est in grano frumenti, post corruptionem ejus et mortem reparat, ac restituit granum in culmi corpus et spicae.
quotes.context: On First Principles 2.10, in Rufinus's Latin (the Greek of this chapter survives only in fragments, some of them quoted by Methodius against him). The abiding ratio, the body's form principle (in the Greek fragments its eidos), is what makes the risen body the same body, though Origen insists it rises spiritual, changed in glory. Quoted from the Lommatzsch witness in the store; the passage still wants a locked library section.

source.edition: Lommatzsch, Origenis Opera Omnia, tomus XXI (Berlin, 1847), De Principiis (Rufinus's Latin)

quotes.author: Methodius of Olympus
quotes.english: God, it seems to me, has arranged the same for us. He saw man, the fairest of his works, ruined by the envious plots of spite, and in his love for mankind he would not leave him so, but dissolved him back into matter, so that in the remoulding everything faulty in him would melt away and vanish. ... What the statue's being melted down is there, that here is the body's dying and dissolution; and what the matter's being shaped again and adorned is there, that here is rising again.
quotes.original: ταὐτὸν γὰρ φαίνεται δή μοι καὶ ἐφ' ἡμῶν ὁ θεὸς διῳκονομηκέναι. τὸν γὰρ ἄνθρωπον, τὸ εὐπρεπέστατον ἑαυτοῦ τέχνημα, βασκάνοις ἐπιβουλαῖς φθόνου κεκακωμένον ἰδὼν οὐκ ἠνέσχετο τοιοῦτον καταλεῖψαι φιλάνθρωπος ὤν, ἀλλὰ διέλυσεν εἰς ὕλην πάλιν, ἵνα διὰ τῆς ἀναπλάσεως ἐκτακῶσι καὶ ἐξαφανισθῶσι πάντα τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ μωμήματα. ... τὸ γὰρ ἐκεῖ ἀναχωνευθῆναι τὸν ἀνδριάντα, τοῦτο ἐνταῦθα τὸ ἀποθανεῖν καὶ διαλυθῆναι τὸ σῶμα, τὸ δὲ ἐκεῖ ἀναμορφοποιηθῆναι τὴν ὕλην ἢ ἀνακοσμηθῆναι, τοῦτο ἐνταῦθα τὸ ἀναστῆναι
quotes.context: Methodius answers Origen in a dialogue (the orthodox speaker is Eubulius). His image is a gold statue, marred by envy, melted down by its maker and cast again in its own form: dissolution is not loss, and the same work comes back without its blemishes. On the Resurrection survives complete only in an Old Slavonic translation; long Greek extracts, this one included, survive because Epiphanius quoted them against the Origenists in Panarion 64 (Migne PG 42). The library's Methodius texts are partly OCR and do not hold this passage.

source.edition: Migne PG 42, Panarion 64 (Methodius, On the Resurrection, quoted)

quotes.author: Augustine of Hippo
quotes.english: The sum of it is this: in the resurrection of the flesh, the size of our bodies will for ever have the measures that the pattern of youth, implanted in each body and still to be perfected or already perfect, once had, with fitting beauty kept in the proportions of every member. ... Only let there be no deformity, no weakness, no slowness and no corruption. ... Whatever has perished from living bodies, or from corpses after death, will be restored.
quotes.original: in resurrectione carnis in aeternum eas mensuras habeat corporum magnitudo, quas habebat perficiendae sive perfectae cuiusque indita corpori ratio iuventutis, in membrorum quoque omnium modulis congruo decore servato ... tantum absit omnis deformitas, omnis infirmitas, omnis tarditas omnisque corruptio ... Restituetur ergo quidquid de corporibus vivis vel post mortem de cadaveribus periit
quotes.context: Augustine's last book works through the objectors' questions one by one: aborted children, bodies eaten or scattered, hair and nails, size and age (22.12-21). His settled answer: nothing of the body is lost to its Maker, defects are removed rather than preserved, and all rise at the measure of grown youth, about the age Christ reached.

gaps.author: Methodius of Olympus
gaps.why: Quoted from the Greek extract Epiphanius preserved in Panarion 64: methodius-resurrection-statue. Still open: On the Resurrection has no library book of its own; the complete text survives in Old Slavonic (Bonwetsch, GCS 27, 1917) and the library's Methodius files do not hold this passage.
